activities.caption: rule or law — file each by what backs it
activities.name: wmlRuleBuckets

config.prompt: Every item here is a rule of some kind — file each by what stands behind it:
buckets: a law — authority, procedure, state backing
a rule, but not a law

items.label: a fashion that spreads until everyone wears it
an Act that survived both Houses and Royal Assent
a statutory instrument under an enabling Act
a by-law of a local authority

config.why: What the shop sign lacks is a recognised authority making the rule by recognised procedures, with the state's backing behind it — and procedures that are themselves law.

activities.caption: stack the sources from top to bottom
activities.name: wmlStackOrder

config.prompt: A lawyer's first skill is knowing which source controls — stack them from the top down:
items: delegated legislation — the executive filling in detail
precedent — what courts said it all means
config.why: Each source trumps the one below — and knowing what to do when two seem to conflict is the rest of the subject.

activities.caption: drag the divider — which way does the causation run?
activities.name: wmlSocietyCompare

config.prompt: Law and society move each other — drag the divider:

before.label: Society changes — law follows
before.text: Statutes on divorce, privacy and data protection appear nowhere in medieval law: the problems are new, so the rules must be.

after.label: Law acts — society follows
after.text: Wearing seatbelts became near-universal within a decade of being required: legal rules both express norms and teach them.

config.why: The relationship runs both directions — studying it means watching which way the causation flows in each case.

activities.anchor: The rule of law is law's own conscience
activities.caption: true or false — validity, fairness, and the three limbs
activities.name: wmlRuleJudge

statements.s: A law can be valid, obeyed and unjust — which is exactly why reform machinery exists.
statements.why: Justice asks whether outcomes are fair; validity is a separate question.

statements.s: Dicey's three limbs include equality before the law — everyone, however powerful, subject to the same law.
statements.why: Alongside no arbitrary power and rights secured by court decisions, not just paper declarations.

statements.s: If it is legal, it must be right.
statements.why: Adultery, lying and ingratitude are legal but widely condemned — the circles overlap without coinciding.

statements.s: Modern formulations such as the World Justice Project index add accessible courts, independent judges and open government.
statements.why: Substance beyond Dicey's form — and the precondition for predictable contracts, investment and daily life.

activities.caption: line up a bill's stages as it grinds toward an Act
activities.name: wmlBillOrder

config.prompt: An idea must survive the whole gauntlet — order the stages:
items: green paper — policy options floated for consultation
white paper — the government's chosen policy
committee stage — line-by-line scrutiny and amendments
config.why: Deliberately slow: public consultation, two chambers and detailed committee scrutiny before anything touches anyone's rights.

activities.anchor: Delegation trades democratic scrutiny for speed
activities.caption: find the line that overstates the delegation
activities.name: wmlDelegatedSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary goes beyond the powers — click it:
lines: Statutory instruments — the technical detail, thousands per year, far outnumbering Acts.
The Privy Council issues orders in council.
Courts can strike delegated legislation down as ultra vires — beyond the parent Act's powers.
Delegated legislation escapes judicial review entirely — only the Joint Committee watches it.
config.correction: Ultra vires review is a real check: an instrument beyond its parent Act can be struck down by the courts.
config.why: Delegation trades scrutiny for speed and expertise — the enabling Act confines it, the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments checks it, and the courts police its outer edge.

activities.caption: pair each reading with the case that shows it
activities.name: wmlMethodsMatch

config.prompt: Four ways in — pair each with the case that shows it:

pairs.right: Whiteley v Chappell (1868): impersonating a dead voter walks free — a dead person is not entitled to vote
Re Sigsworth (1935): the murderer son denied the inheritance the plain words seemed to grant
Heydon's Case (1584): read the statute to cure the defect it targeted
the Human Rights Act 1998: read compatibly with Convention rights where possible

config.why: The same sentence can license any of the four readings, and which one wins decides real cases — presumptions and internal aids (long title, schedules) run alongside.

activities.anchor: Precedent is the common law system's compounding technology
activities.caption: fill the binding part and the by-the-way part
activities.name: wmlPrecedentCloze

config.text: The binding part is the %%ratio decidendi%% — the rule that justified the outcome — while everything else a judge says (%%obiter dicta%%, "by the way") only persuades. Distinguishing is the safety valve; overruling is reserved to higher courts because predictability is the point.
config.hint: One is "the reason for deciding"; the other is Latin for "said by the way".
